0How to work a problem

Six named steps for every calculation

Each problem in this tutorial is worked in named steps. The names tell you what the step is for, so you can use the same pattern on new problems.

  1. Read and sketch. Draw the mechanism or system and mark what moves.
  2. List the data. Write each given value with its symbol and unit. The "Given" table on each problem does this for you.
  3. Convert to SI units. Millimetres to metres, rpm to rad/s, kN to N, degrees to radians where a formula needs them.
  4. Choose the relation. Name the law or formula and say why it applies.
  5. Substitute and work out. Put the numbers in, one quantity at a time, keeping three or four significant figures.
  6. Check and state the answer. Check the units and whether the size is sensible, then give the answer with its unit and direction.

Problem 1.1 Mobility of a four-bar linkage

A four-bar linkage has four links (the fixed frame, the crank, the coupler and the rocker) joined by four pin joints. Find its mobility.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Number of links, frame includedNNN4
Lower pairs (pin joints)P1P_1P1​4
Higher pairsP2P_2P2​0

Find

  • The mobility FFF and what it means for driving the linkage

Terms used in this problem

Link
one rigid part of the mechanism. The fixed frame is a link too and must be counted.
Pair (joint)
the connection between two links that lets them move relative to each other in a set way.
Lower pair
a pair with surface contact, such as a pin (turning) or a slider (sliding). It leaves 1 freedom and removes 2.
Higher pair
a pair with point or line contact, such as a cam on its follower or two gear teeth. It removes 1 freedom.
Mobility FFF
the number of separate inputs needed to fix the position of every link (also called the degrees of freedom).
Kutzbach criterion
the counting rule for plane mechanisms. Each moving link has 3 freedoms in a plane (two slides and one turn); the joints take some away.

Solution

  1. Step 1Count the links

    Include the fixed frame.

    N=4N = 4N=4
  2. Step 2Count the pairs by type

    Four pin joints are lower pairs; there is no cam or gear contact.

    P1=4,P2=0P_1 = 4,\qquad P_2 = 0P1​=4,P2​=0
  3. Step 3Apply the Kutzbach criterion

    Three freedoms for each of the N−1N-1N−1 moving links, less two for each lower pair and one for each higher pair.

    F=3(N−1)−2P1−P2F = 3(N-1) - 2P_1 - P_2F=3(N−1)−2P1​−P2​
    F=3(4−1)−2(4)−0=9−8=1F = 3(4-1) - 2(4) - 0 = 9 - 8 = 1F=3(4−1)−2(4)−0=9−8=1
  4. Step 4Read the result

    F=1F = 1F=1: one input, turning the crank, fixes the position of every other link. F=0F = 0F=0 would be a rigid structure and F=2F = 2F=2 would need two inputs.

Answer F=1F = 1F=1. The four-bar is a constrained mechanism driven by one input.

Commonest error: leaving out the frame, so that N=3N = 3N=3 and F=3(2)−8=−2F = 3(2) - 8 = -2F=3(2)−8=−2.

Problem 1.2 Mobility with a higher pair (cam and follower)

A cam and a follower are each pinned to the frame, and the cam touches the follower. Find the mobility.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Number of links: frame, cam, followerNNN3
Lower pairs: two pins to the frameP1P_1P1​2
Higher pairs: cam on followerP2P_2P2​1

Find

  • The mobility FFF

Terms used in this problem

Cam
a shaped plate or disc that pushes a follower as it turns.
Follower
the link that rides on the cam and copies its profile as motion.
Higher pair
point or line contact; the follower can both roll and slide on the cam, so only 1 freedom is removed.
Kutzbach criterion
F=3(N−1)−2P1−P2F = 3(N-1) - 2P_1 - P_2F=3(N−1)−2P1​−P2​, as in Problem 1.1.

Solution

  1. Step 1Count the links

    Frame, cam and follower.

    N=3N = 3N=3
  2. Step 2Count the pairs by type

    The two pins are lower pairs; the cam contact is a higher pair.

    P1=2,P2=1P_1 = 2,\qquad P_2 = 1P1​=2,P2​=1
  3. Step 3Apply the Kutzbach criterion
    F=3(3−1)−2(2)−1=6−4−1=1F = 3(3-1) - 2(2) - 1 = 6 - 4 - 1 = 1F=3(3−1)−2(2)−1=6−4−1=1

Answer F=1F = 1F=1. Turning the cam fixes the follower position.

A higher pair removes only one freedom, which is why the count still gives one.

Problem 1.3 Piston and connecting-rod velocity

In a slider-crank, the crank is 50 mm long and turns at 20 rad/s. The connecting rod is 200 mm long. At a crank angle of 60° from top dead centre, find the piston velocity and the angular velocity of the rod.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Crank radiusrrr50 mm = 0.05 m
Crank angular velocityω\omegaω20 rad/s
Connecting-rod lengthLLL200 mm = 0.2 m
Crank angle from TDCθ\thetaθ60°

Find

  • Piston velocity vPv_PvP​
  • Rod angular velocity ωAB\omega_{AB}ωAB​

Terms used in this problem

Crank
the arm that turns about the main shaft; its end is the crank pin AAA.
Connecting rod
the link from the crank pin AAA to the piston (gudgeon) pin BBB.
Top dead centre (TDC)
the position where crank and rod are in line and the piston is farthest from the crankshaft. θ\thetaθ is measured from here.
Ratio nnn
rod length over crank radius, n=L/rn = L/rn=L/r.
Obliquity angle ϕ\phiϕ
the angle the connecting rod makes with the line of stroke.
Angular velocity
rate of turning in rad/s. A point at radius rrr moves at ωr\omega rωr at right angles to the radius.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the crank-pin velocity

    The crank pin moves on a circle, at right angles to the crank.

    vA=ωr=20×0.05=1.0 m/sv_A = \omega r = 20 \times 0.05 = 1.0\ \text{m/s}vA​=ωr=20×0.05=1.0 m/s
  2. Step 2Find the ratio nnn
    n=Lr=20050=4n = \frac{L}{r} = \frac{200}{50} = 4n=rL​=50200​=4
  3. Step 3Find the piston velocity

    The second term in the bracket corrects for the slope of the rod (obliquity); it vanishes for a very long rod.

    vP=ωr(sin⁡θ+sin⁡2θ2n)v_P = \omega r\left(\sin\theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2n}\right)vP​=ωr(sinθ+2nsin2θ​)
    vP=1.0(0.8660+0.86608)=0.974 m/sv_P = 1.0\left(0.8660 + \frac{0.8660}{8}\right) = 0.974\ \text{m/s}vP​=1.0(0.8660+80.8660​)=0.974 m/s

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the rod angle

    From the triangle of crank and rod, Lsin⁡ϕ=rsin⁡θL\sin\phi = r\sin\thetaLsinϕ=rsinθ.

    sin⁡ϕ=sin⁡θn=0.86604=0.2165,ϕ=12.50∘\sin\phi = \frac{\sin\theta}{n} = \frac{0.8660}{4} = 0.2165,\qquad \phi = 12.50^\circsinϕ=nsinθ​=40.8660​=0.2165,ϕ=12.50∘
  2. Step 5Find the rod angular velocity
    ωAB=ωrcos⁡θLcos⁡ϕ=20×0.05×0.50.2×0.9763=2.56 rad/s\omega_{AB} = \frac{\omega r\cos\theta}{L\cos\phi} = \frac{20 \times 0.05 \times 0.5}{0.2 \times 0.9763} = 2.56\ \text{rad/s}ωAB​=Lcosϕωrcosθ​=0.2×0.976320×0.05×0.5​=2.56 rad/s

Answer vP=0.974v_P = 0.974vP​=0.974 m/s and ωAB=2.56\omega_{AB} = 2.56ωAB​=2.56 rad/s.

Problem 1.4 Output speed from instantaneous centres

A four-bar has crank speed ω2=10\omega_2 = 10ω2​=10 rad/s. Measured on the drawing, I12I24=90I_{12}I_{24} = 90I12​I24​=90 mm and I14I24=150I_{14}I_{24} = 150I14​I24​=150 mm. Find the angular velocity ω4\omega_4ω4​ of the output link.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Crank (link 2) speedω2\omega_2ω2​10 rad/s
Distance from crank pivot to the common centreI12I24I_{12}I_{24}I12​I24​90 mm
Distance from output pivot to the common centreI14I24I_{14}I_{24}I14​I24​150 mm

Find

  • Output angular velocity ω4\omega_4ω4​

Terms used in this problem

Instantaneous centre IijI_{ij}Iij​
the point about which link iii is turning relative to link jjj at this instant. It is also a point that has the same velocity whether it is taken on link iii or on link jjj.
I12I_{12}I12​ and I14I_{14}I14​
the fixed pivots of the crank (link 2) and the output (link 4) on the frame (link 1).
I24I_{24}I24​
the instantaneous centre of the crank and the output, found by Kennedy's theorem.
Kennedy's theorem
the three instantaneous centres of any three links lie on one straight line.

Solution

  1. Step 1Pick the common point

    I24I_{24}I24​ belongs to both link 2 and link 4, so its velocity is the same on both.

  2. Step 2Write its velocity two ways

    As a point on link 2 it turns about I12I_{12}I12​; as a point on link 4 it turns about I14I_{14}I14​.

    ω2×I12I24=ω4×I14I24\omega_2 \times I_{12}I_{24} = \omega_4 \times I_{14}I_{24}ω2​×I12​I24​=ω4​×I14​I24​
  3. Step 3Solve for the output speed
    ω4=10×90150=6 rad/s\omega_4 = \frac{10 \times 90}{150} = 6\ \text{rad/s}ω4​=15010×90​=6 rad/s
  4. Step 4Find the sense of rotation

    If I24I_{24}I24​ lies outside the line between I12I_{12}I12​ and I14I_{14}I14​, links 2 and 4 turn the same way; if it lies between them, they turn opposite ways.

Answer ω4=6\omega_4 = 6ω4​=6 rad/s. The speed ratio is the inverse ratio of the distances of I24I_{24}I24​ from the two fixed pivots; no velocity polygon is needed.

Problem 1.5 Piston acceleration

For the slider-crank of Problem 1.3 (r=50r = 50r=50 mm, L=200L = 200L=200 mm, ω=20\omega = 20ω=20 rad/s constant, θ=60∘\theta = 60^\circθ=60∘), find the piston acceleration, and compare its values at the two dead centres.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Crank radiusrrr0.05 m
Crank speed (constant)ω\omegaω20 rad/s
Ration=L/rn = L/rn=L/r4
Crank angleθ\thetaθ60°

Find

  • Piston acceleration aPa_PaP​ at 60°, at TDC and at BDC

Terms used in this problem

Centripetal acceleration
ω2r\omega^2 rω2r, directed towards the centre of the circle. It is the only acceleration of the crank pin when ω\omegaω is constant.
Bottom dead centre (BDC)
the other in-line position, θ=180∘\theta = 180^\circθ=180∘, with the piston nearest the crankshaft.
Sign of aPa_PaP​
positive means towards the crankshaft (the direction the piston moves just after TDC).

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the crank-pin acceleration

    Constant speed, so there is no tangential part.

    ω2r=202×0.05=20 m/s2\omega^2 r = 20^2 \times 0.05 = 20\ \text{m/s}^2ω2r=202×0.05=20 m/s2
  2. Step 2Find the piston acceleration

    As for velocity, the cos⁡2θ/n\cos 2\theta / ncos2θ/n term is the obliquity correction.

    aP=ω2r(cos⁡θ+cos⁡2θn)a_P = \omega^2 r\left(\cos\theta + \frac{\cos 2\theta}{n}\right)aP​=ω2r(cosθ+ncos2θ​)
    aP=20(0.5+−0.54)=20×0.375=7.5 m/s2a_P = 20\left(0.5 + \frac{-0.5}{4}\right) = 20 \times 0.375 = 7.5\ \text{m/s}^2aP​=20(0.5+4−0.5​)=20×0.375=7.5 m/s2
  3. Step 3Evaluate at the dead centres

    Put θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 and θ=180∘\theta = 180^\circθ=180∘.

    TDC: a=ω2r(1+1n)=20×1.25=25 m/s2\text{TDC: } a = \omega^2 r\left(1 + \tfrac1n\right) = 20 \times 1.25 = 25\ \text{m/s}^2TDC: a=ω2r(1+n1​)=20×1.25=25 m/s2
    BDC: a=ω2r(−1+1n)=20×(−0.75)=−15 m/s2\text{BDC: } a = \omega^2 r\left(-1 + \tfrac1n\right) = 20 \times (-0.75) = -15\ \text{m/s}^2BDC: a=ω2r(−1+n1​)=20×(−0.75)=−15 m/s2

Answer aP=7.5a_P = 7.5aP​=7.5 m/s² at 60°; 25 m/s² at TDC and −15 m/s² at BDC.

The two ends differ because of the rod obliquity. This unequal acceleration is what makes the inertia forces of Topic 2.

Short problems

1.AA linkage has 5 links (frame included), 5 pin joints and 1 higher pair. Find its mobility.

Term: Mobility: number of inputs needed to fix the motion.

  1. Step 1Apply Kutzbach
    F=3(5−1)−2(5)−1=12−10−1=1F = 3(5-1) - 2(5) - 1 = 12 - 10 - 1 = 1F=3(5−1)−2(5)−1=12−10−1=1

Answer F=1F = 1F=1.

1.BA block slides outwards at 0.8 m/s along a slotted lever that turns at 5 rad/s. Find the Coriolis component of its acceleration.

Term: Coriolis component: the extra acceleration of a point that slides along a link while the link turns.

  1. Step 1Apply the Coriolis formula
    ac=2ωv=2×5×0.8=8 m/s2a_c = 2\omega v = 2 \times 5 \times 0.8 = 8\ \text{m/s}^2ac​=2ωv=2×5×0.8=8 m/s2
  2. Step 2Find its direction
    at 90∘ to the lever\text{at } 90^\circ \text{ to the lever}at 90∘ to the lever

Answer 8 m/s², perpendicular to the lever.

1.CHow many instantaneous centres does a six-link mechanism have?

Term: Each pair of links has one instantaneous centre.

  1. Step 1Count the pairs of links
    N=n(n−1)2=6×52=15N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15N=2n(n−1)​=26×5​=15

Answer 15.

Problem 2.1 Inertia torque from a connecting rod

A vertical engine has a connecting rod 2 m long between centres, of mass 250 kg, with its mass centre 800 mm from the big end. Hung as a pendulum from the gudgeon pin, it makes 8 complete swings in 22 s. The crank is 400 mm long and turns at 200 rpm. Find the radius of gyration of the rod about its mass centre, and the inertia torque on the crankshaft when the crank is 40° past TDC with the piston moving down.

Rattan (2009), Example 13.8

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Rod length between centreslll2 m
Rod massmmm250 kg
Big end to GGG0.8 m
Swings and time8 in 22 s
Crank radiusrrr0.4 m
Crank speedNNN200 rpm
Crank angleθ\thetaθ40°

Find

  • Radius of gyration kGk_GkG​
  • Inertia torque TTT on the crankshaft

Terms used in this problem

Big end and small end
the big end of the rod goes on the crank pin AAA; the small end goes on the gudgeon (piston) pin BBB.
Mass centre GGG
the point where the whole mass of the rod can be taken to act.
Compound pendulum
a solid body swinging about a pivot; here the rod hung from the gudgeon pin.
Equivalent length LLL
the length of a simple pendulum (point mass on a string) with the same period: tp=2πL/gt_p = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}tp​=2πL/g​.
Radius of gyration kGk_GkG​
the radius at which the whole mass could sit and give the same moment of inertia: IG=mkG2I_G = m k_G^2IG​=mkG2​.
Two-mass system
the rod replaced by two point masses, one at each end, with the same total mass and the same mass centre.
Correction couple ΔT\Delta TΔT
the extra torque needed because two masses at the ends do not have the rod's true moment of inertia.
Inertia force
the force −ma-ma−ma (d'Alembert) that a mass "pushes back" with when it is accelerated.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the distance from GGG to the small end

    The rod swings about the gudgeon pin, so we need bbb, the distance from the pivot to GGG.

    b=l−0.8=2−0.8=1.2 mb = l - 0.8 = 2 - 0.8 = 1.2\ \text{m}b=l−0.8=2−0.8=1.2 m
  2. Step 2Find the period of one swing
    tp=228=2.75 st_p = \frac{22}{8} = 2.75\ \text{s}tp​=822​=2.75 s
  3. Step 3Find the equivalent pendulum length

    From tp=2πL/gt_p = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}tp​=2πL/g​:

    L=g(tp2π)2=9.81(2.752π)2=1.879 mL = g\left(\frac{t_p}{2\pi}\right)^2 = 9.81\left(\frac{2.75}{2\pi}\right)^2 = 1.879\ \text{m}L=g(2πtp​​)2=9.81(2π2.75​)2=1.879 m
  4. Step 4Find the radius of gyration

    For a compound pendulum L=b+kG2/bL = b + k_G^2/bL=b+kG2​/b, so:

    kG2=b(L−b)=1.2×0.679=0.815 m2,kG=0.903 mk_G^2 = b(L - b) = 1.2 \times 0.679 = 0.815\ \text{m}^2,\qquad k_G = 0.903\ \text{m}kG2​=b(L−b)=1.2×0.679=0.815 m2,kG​=0.903 m
  5. Step 5Split the rod mass between the two ends

    Each end takes the share that keeps GGG in place: the end nearer GGG takes more.

    ma=m bl=250×1.22=150 kg (crank pin),mb=100 kg (gudgeon pin)m_a = \frac{m\,b}{l} = \frac{250 \times 1.2}{2} = 150\ \text{kg (crank pin)},\qquad m_b = 100\ \text{kg (gudgeon pin)}ma​=lmb​=2250×1.2​=150 kg (crank pin),mb​=100 kg (gudgeon pin)

Solution, continued

  1. Step 6Find the crank speed and nnn
    ω=2πN60=2π×20060=20.94 rad/s,n=lr=20.4=5\omega = \frac{2\pi N}{60} = \frac{2\pi \times 200}{60} = 20.94\ \text{rad/s},\qquad n = \frac{l}{r} = \frac{2}{0.4} = 5ω=602πN​=602π×200​=20.94 rad/s,n=rl​=0.42​=5
  2. Step 7Find the inertia force of the mass at the gudgeon pin

    It moves with the piston, so it uses the piston acceleration of Problem 1.5. Its weight acts against this force here.

    Fb=mb ω2r(cos⁡θ+cos⁡2θn)=100×438.6×0.4×0.8008=14 050 NF_b = m_b\,\omega^2 r\left(\cos\theta + \frac{\cos 2\theta}{n}\right) = 100 \times 438.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.8008 = 14\,050\ \text{N}Fb​=mb​ω2r(cosθ+ncos2θ​)=100×438.6×0.4×0.8008=14050 N
    Fnet=14 050−mbg=14 050−981=13 069 NF_{net} = 14\,050 - m_b g = 14\,050 - 981 = 13\,069\ \text{N}Fnet​=14050−mb​g=14050−981=13069 N
  3. Step 8Turn this force into a crank torque

    The bracket converts a force along the line of stroke into torque on the crank.

    Tb=Fnet r(sin⁡θ+sin⁡2θ2n2−sin⁡2θ)=13 069×0.4×0.7421=3879 N mT_b = F_{net}\, r\left(\sin\theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2\sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2\theta}}\right) = 13\,069 \times 0.4 \times 0.7421 = 3879\ \text{N m}Tb​=Fnet​r(sinθ+2n2−sin2θ​sin2θ​)=13069×0.4×0.7421=3879 N m

Solution, continued

  1. Step 9Find the rod angular acceleration
    αc=−ω2sin⁡θ n2−1(n2−sin⁡2θ)3/2=−438.6×0.6428×24121.9=−55.5 rad/s2\alpha_c = -\omega^2 \sin\theta\,\frac{n^2 - 1}{(n^2 - \sin^2\theta)^{3/2}} = -438.6 \times 0.6428 \times \frac{24}{121.9} = -55.5\ \text{rad/s}^2αc​=−ω2sinθ(n2−sin2θ)3/2n2−1​=−438.6×0.6428×121.924​=−55.5 rad/s2
  2. Step 10Find the correction torque

    The correction couple acts on the rod; the second line carries it to the crankshaft.

    ΔT=m b αc (l−L)=250×1.2×(−55.5)×(2−1.879)=−2011 N m\Delta T = m\,b\,\alpha_c\,(l - L) = 250 \times 1.2 \times (-55.5) \times (2 - 1.879) = -2011\ \text{N m}ΔT=mbαc​(l−L)=250×1.2×(−55.5)×(2−1.879)=−2011 N m
    Tc=ΔTcos⁡θn2−sin⁡2θ=−2011×0.7664.959=−310.7 N mT_c = \frac{\Delta T\cos\theta}{\sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2\theta}} = \frac{-2011 \times 0.766}{4.959} = -310.7\ \text{N m}Tc​=n2−sin2θ​ΔTcosθ​=4.959−2011×0.766​=−310.7 N m
  3. Step 11Find the torque from the weight at the crank pin
    Ta=ma g rsin⁡θ=150×9.81×0.4×0.6428=378.3 N mT_a = m_a\, g\, r \sin\theta = 150 \times 9.81 \times 0.4 \times 0.6428 = 378.3\ \text{N m}Ta​=ma​grsinθ=150×9.81×0.4×0.6428=378.3 N m
  4. Step 12Add the three torques

    Signs as in Rattan: TcT_cTc​ is subtracted (it is negative, so it adds), and the weight torque opposes the inertia torque at this angle.

    T=Tb−Tc−Ta=3879+310.7−378.3=3812 N mT = T_b - T_c - T_a = 3879 + 310.7 - 378.3 = 3812\ \text{N m}T=Tb​−Tc​−Ta​=3879+310.7−378.3=3812 N m

Answer kG=0.903k_G = 0.903kG​=0.903 m; inertia torque about 3810 N m (Rattan gives 3809.5 N m from rounded figures).

Problem 2.2 Net turning moment with gas pressure

For the engine of Problem 2.1, the cylinder bore is 700 mm, the gas pressure is 600 kN/m² and the piston has a mass of 120 kg. Find the turning moment on the crankshaft at the same crank position.

Rattan (2009), Example 13.9

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
BoreDDD0.7 m
Gas pressureppp600 kN/m²
Piston mass120 kg
From Problem 2.1mb=100m_b = 100mb​=100 kg, ω2r=175.5\omega^2 r = 175.5ω2r=175.5 m/s², bracket 0.8008, torque factor 0.7421, Tc=−310.7T_c = -310.7Tc​=−310.7 N m, Ta=378.3T_a = 378.3Ta​=378.3 N m

Find

  • Turning moment TTT available at the crankshaft

Terms used in this problem

Reciprocating mass
all mass that moves up and down with the piston: the piston itself plus the rod share at the gudgeon pin.
Gas force
pressure times piston area, pushing the piston down on the power stroke.
Torque factor
sin⁡θ+sin⁡2θ/(2n2−sin⁡2θ)\sin\theta + \sin 2\theta/(2\sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2\theta})sinθ+sin2θ/(2n2−sin2θ​), which turns a force on the piston into crank torque per metre of crank.
Turning moment
the net torque the crankshaft receives: gas torque less the torque used to accelerate the moving parts.

Solution

  1. Step 1Add up the reciprocating mass
    mR=100+120=220 kgm_R = 100 + 120 = 220\ \text{kg}mR​=100+120=220 kg
  2. Step 2Find its inertia force

    As in Problem 2.1, only the rod share of weight (981 N) is subtracted, following Rattan.

    FI=220×175.5×0.8008=30 911 N,Fnet=30 911−981=29 930 NF_I = 220 \times 175.5 \times 0.8008 = 30\,911\ \text{N},\qquad F_{net} = 30\,911 - 981 = 29\,930\ \text{N}FI​=220×175.5×0.8008=30911 N,Fnet​=30911−981=29930 N
  3. Step 3Find the total inertia torque

    Turn the force into torque, then add the correction and weight torques from Problem 2.1.

    TI=29 930×0.4×0.7421=8884 N mT_I = 29\,930 \times 0.4 \times 0.7421 = 8884\ \text{N m}TI​=29930×0.4×0.7421=8884 N m
    TI+310.7−378.3=8817 N mT_I + 310.7 - 378.3 = 8817\ \text{N m}TI​+310.7−378.3=8817 N m

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the gas force
    A=πD24=π×0.724=0.3848 m2,Fg=pA=600 000×0.3848=230 907 NA = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 0.7^2}{4} = 0.3848\ \text{m}^2,\qquad F_g = pA = 600\,000 \times 0.3848 = 230\,907\ \text{N}A=4πD2​=4π×0.72​=0.3848 m2,Fg​=pA=600000×0.3848=230907 N
  2. Step 5Find the gas torque
    Tg=230 907×0.4×0.7421=68 542 N mT_g = 230\,907 \times 0.4 \times 0.7421 = 68\,542\ \text{N m}Tg​=230907×0.4×0.7421=68542 N m
  3. Step 6Subtract the inertia torque

    The piston is speeding up downwards, so its inertia force acts upwards, against the gas force.

    T=68 542−8817=59 725 N mT = 68\,542 - 8817 = 59\,725\ \text{N m}T=68542−8817=59725 N m

Answer About 59.7 kN m.

Counting the piston weight as well (1177 N) would lower the inertia torque by a further 349 N m.

Problem 2.3 Coefficient of fluctuation of speed from a turning-moment diagram

The turning-moment diagram of a petrol engine is drawn to scales of 1 mm = 500 N m and 1 mm = 3°, and repeats every half revolution. The areas above and below the mean torque line, in order, are +260, −580, +80, −380, +870 and −250 mm². The rotating parts have a mass of 55 kg and a radius of gyration of 2.1 m. At 1600 rpm, find the coefficient of fluctuation of speed.

Rattan (2009), Example 13.16

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Torque scale1 mm = 500 N m
Angle scale1 mm = 3°
Areas in order (mm²)+260, −580, +80, −380, +870, −250
Mass of rotating partsmmm55 kg
Radius of gyrationkkk2.1 m
Mean speedNNN1600 rpm

Find

  • Coefficient of fluctuation of speed KKK

Terms used in this problem

Turning-moment diagram
a graph of crankshaft torque against crank angle; area under it is work (energy).
Mean torque line
the steady torque that the load takes. Area above it is surplus energy that speeds the flywheel up; area below is a deficit that slows it.
Maximum fluctuation of energy eee
the difference between the greatest and least energy reached in the cycle.
Coefficient of fluctuation of speed KKK
the speed range divided by the mean speed, K=(ωmax−ωmin)/ωK = (\omega_{max} - \omega_{min})/\omegaK=(ωmax​−ωmin​)/ω.
Mass moment of inertia III
resistance to angular acceleration, I=mk2I = m k^2I=mk2 in kg m².

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the energy of 1 mm² of diagram

    Torque times angle in radians gives joules.

    1 mm2=500×3×π180=26.18 J1\ \text{mm}^2 = 500 \times 3 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = 26.18\ \text{J}1 mm2=500×3×180π​=26.18 J
  2. Step 2Track the energy round the cycle

    Start at EEE and add each area in turn: EEE, E+260E+260E+260, E−320E-320E−320, E−240E-240E−240, E−620E-620E−620, E+250E+250E+250, EEE. The cycle closes, which checks the areas.

  3. Step 3Find the maximum fluctuation of energy

    Greatest E+260E + 260E+260, least E−620E - 620E−620.

    e=260−(−620)=880 mm2=880×26.18=23 038 Je = 260 - (-620) = 880\ \text{mm}^2 = 880 \times 26.18 = 23\,038\ \text{J}e=260−(−620)=880 mm2=880×26.18=23038 J
  4. Step 4Find the speed and the inertia
    ω=2π×160060=167.6 rad/s,I=mk2=55×2.12=242.6 kg m2\omega = \frac{2\pi \times 1600}{60} = 167.6\ \text{rad/s},\qquad I = m k^2 = 55 \times 2.1^2 = 242.6\ \text{kg m}^2ω=602π×1600​=167.6 rad/s,I=mk2=55×2.12=242.6 kg m2
  5. Step 5Find KKK

    From e=12I(ωmax2−ωmin2)=Iω2Ke = \tfrac12 I(\omega_{max}^2 - \omega_{min}^2) = I\omega^2 Ke=21​I(ωmax2​−ωmin2​)=Iω2K:

    K=eIω2=23 038242.6×167.62=0.0034K = \frac{e}{I\omega^2} = \frac{23\,038}{242.6 \times 167.6^2} = 0.0034K=Iω2e​=242.6×167.6223038​=0.0034

Answer K=0.0034K = 0.0034K=0.0034, that is the speed varies by 0.34% of the mean.

Problem 2.4 Energy stored by a flywheel

A flywheel of mass 3000 kg has a radius of gyration of 1.6 m. Find the energy it stores when its speed rises from 315 rpm to 340 rpm.

Rattan (2009), Example 13.12

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Massmmm3000 kg
Radius of gyrationkkk1.6 m
Speeds315 rpm and 340 rpm

Find

  • Energy stored

Terms used in this problem

Kinetic energy of rotation
12Iω2\tfrac12 I\omega^221​Iω2, with I=mk2I = mk^2I=mk2.
Energy stored
the rise in kinetic energy between the two speeds.
rpm to rad/s
ω=2πN/60\omega = 2\pi N/60ω=2πN/60.

Solution

  1. Step 1Convert the speeds to rad/s
    ω1=2π×34060=35.60 rad/s,ω2=2π×31560=32.99 rad/s\omega_1 = \frac{2\pi \times 340}{60} = 35.60\ \text{rad/s},\qquad \omega_2 = \frac{2\pi \times 315}{60} = 32.99\ \text{rad/s}ω1​=602π×340​=35.60 rad/s,ω2​=602π×315​=32.99 rad/s
  2. Step 2Find the moment of inertia
    I=mk2=3000×1.62=7680 kg m2I = m k^2 = 3000 \times 1.6^2 = 7680\ \text{kg m}^2I=mk2=3000×1.62=7680 kg m2
  3. Step 3Find the change of kinetic energy
    ΔE=12I(ω12−ω22)=12×7680×(35.602−32.992)=689.6 kJ\Delta E = \tfrac12 I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2) = \tfrac12 \times 7680 \times (35.60^2 - 32.99^2) = 689.6\ \text{kJ}ΔE=21​I(ω12​−ω22​)=21​×7680×(35.602−32.992)=689.6 kJ

Answer About 689.6 kJ. (Rattan rounds the speeds to 35.6 and 33 rad/s and gets 684.9 kJ.)

The book states the flywheel as "3 kN". Read as a weight, the mass would be 306 kg and the energy 70.3 kJ. Always check whether a figure is a mass or a weight.

Problem 2.5 Kinetic energy from energy absorbed

A flywheel absorbs 24 kJ when its speed rises from 210 rpm to 214 rpm. Find its kinetic energy at 250 rpm.

Rattan (2009), Example 13.13

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Energy absorbed24 kJ
Speed change210 to 214 rpm
Speed asked about250 rpm

Find

  • Kinetic energy EEE at 250 rpm

Terms used in this problem

Kinetic energy of rotation
12Iω2\tfrac12 I\omega^221​Iω2, the energy a spinning wheel holds; III is its moment of inertia.
Energy absorbed
the rise in kinetic energy, 12I(ω22−ω12)\tfrac12 I(\omega_2^2 - \omega_1^2)21​I(ω22​−ω12​).
Ratio method
dividing two equations so that the unknown III cancels.

Solution

  1. Step 1Write the energy absorbed

    Since ω=2πN/60\omega = 2\pi N/60ω=2πN/60, the factor (2π/60)2(2\pi/60)^2(2π/60)2 appears in both equations.

    24 000=12I(2π60)2(2142−2102)24\,000 = \tfrac12 I\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{60}\right)^2 (214^2 - 210^2)24000=21​I(602π​)2(2142−2102)
  2. Step 2Write the energy at 250 rpm
    E=12I(2π60)2×2502E = \tfrac12 I\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{60}\right)^2 \times 250^2E=21​I(602π​)2×2502
  3. Step 3Divide to cancel III
    E24 000=25022142−2102=62 5001696,E=884.4 kJ\frac{E}{24\,000} = \frac{250^2}{214^2 - 210^2} = \frac{62\,500}{1696},\qquad E = 884.4\ \text{kJ}24000E​=2142−21022502​=169662500​,E=884.4 kJ

Answer E=884.4E = 884.4E=884.4 kJ.

Problem 2.6 Flywheel mass for a steam engine

A double-acting steam engine develops 56 kW at 210 rpm. The greatest and least speeds stay within 1% of the mean, and the excess energy is 30% of the work per stroke. Find the flywheel mass for a radius of gyration of 500 mm.

Rattan (2009), Example 13.14

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
PowerPPP56 kW
SpeedNNN210 rpm
Speed limits±1% of mean
Excess energy30% of work per stroke
Radius of gyrationkkk0.5 m

Find

  • Flywheel mass mmm

Terms used in this problem

Double-acting
steam acts on both sides of the piston, so there are two working strokes per revolution.
Work per stroke
the work done in one working stroke: power divided by strokes per second.
Excess energy eee
the maximum fluctuation of energy the flywheel must absorb and give back.
KKK
coefficient of fluctuation of speed; ±1% gives K=0.02K = 0.02K=0.02.

Solution

  1. Step 1Count the working strokes
    2×210=420 strokes per minute=7 per second2 \times 210 = 420\ \text{strokes per minute} = 7\ \text{per second}2×210=420 strokes per minute=7 per second
  2. Step 2Find the work per stroke
    W=56 0007=8000 JW = \frac{56\,000}{7} = 8000\ \text{J}W=756000​=8000 J
  3. Step 3Find the excess energy and KKK
    e=0.3×8000=2400 J,K=1.01−0.99=0.02e = 0.3 \times 8000 = 2400\ \text{J},\qquad K = 1.01 - 0.99 = 0.02e=0.3×8000=2400 J,K=1.01−0.99=0.02
  4. Step 4Find the mean speed
    ω=2π×21060=21.99 rad/s\omega = \frac{2\pi \times 210}{60} = 21.99\ \text{rad/s}ω=602π×210​=21.99 rad/s
  5. Step 5Find the mass

    From e=Iω2Ke = I\omega^2 Ke=Iω2K with I=mk2I = mk^2I=mk2:

    m=ek2ω2K=24000.52×21.992×0.02=992 kgm = \frac{e}{k^2\omega^2 K} = \frac{2400}{0.5^2 \times 21.99^2 \times 0.02} = 992\ \text{kg}m=k2ω2Ke​=0.52×21.992×0.022400​=992 kg

Answer m=992m = 992m=992 kg.

Problem 2.7 Designing a cast-iron flywheel rim

Design a rim flywheel for the engine of Problem 2.6 (e=2400e = 2400e=2400 J, K=0.02K = 0.02K=0.02, 210 rpm). Take a density of 7200 kg/m³, a safe hoop stress of 6 MPa, and a rim width twice its thickness. Assume the rim gives all the inertia.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Excess energyeee2400 J
Coefficient of fluctuationKKK0.02
SpeedNNN210 rpm (21.99 rad/s)
Safe stressσ\sigmaσ6 MPa
Densityρ\rhoρ7200 kg/m³
Sectionwidth b=2tb = 2tb=2t

Find

  • Rim mean radius, mass and section size

Terms used in this problem

Rim
the heavy outer ring of the flywheel; arms and hub are neglected here.
Hoop stress
tension around the spinning rim, σ=ρv2\sigma = \rho v^2σ=ρv2, where vvv is the rim speed. It limits the size of the wheel.
Rim speed vvv
speed of the rim at its mean radius, v=ωrv = \omega rv=ωr.
Section area AAA
cross-section of the rim, width bbb times thickness ttt.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the moment of inertia needed
    I=eKω2=24000.02×21.992=248.1 kg m2I = \frac{e}{K\omega^2} = \frac{2400}{0.02 \times 21.99^2} = 248.1\ \text{kg m}^2I=Kω2e​=0.02×21.9922400​=248.1 kg m2
  2. Step 2Find the safe rim speed

    From σ=ρv2\sigma = \rho v^2σ=ρv2:

    v=σρ=6×1067200=28.87 m/sv = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{6 \times 10^6}{7200}} = 28.87\ \text{m/s}v=ρσ​​=72006×106​​=28.87 m/s
  3. Step 3Find the mean radius
    r=vω=28.8721.99=1.313 m (diameter 2.63 m)r = \frac{v}{\omega} = \frac{28.87}{21.99} = 1.313\ \text{m (diameter 2.63 m)}r=ωv​=21.9928.87​=1.313 m (diameter 2.63 m)

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the rim mass

    All the mass is at radius rrr, so I=mr2I = m r^2I=mr2.

    m=Ir2=248.11.3132=144 kgm = \frac{I}{r^2} = \frac{248.1}{1.313^2} = 144\ \text{kg}m=r2I​=1.3132248.1​=144 kg
  2. Step 5Find the section

    Mass = density × circumference × area; then bt=2t2b t = 2t^2bt=2t2.

    A=m2πrρ=1442π×1.313×7200=2425 mm2A = \frac{m}{2\pi r\rho} = \frac{144}{2\pi \times 1.313 \times 7200} = 2425\ \text{mm}^2A=2πrρm​=2π×1.313×7200144​=2425 mm2
    t=A/2=34.8 mm,b=69.6 mmt = \sqrt{A/2} = 34.8\ \text{mm},\qquad b = 69.6\ \text{mm}t=A/2​=34.8 mm,b=69.6 mm

Answer A rim of 2.63 m diameter, 144 kg, about 35 mm thick and 70 mm wide.

Problem 2.6 used a 0.5 m radius of gyration and needed 992 kg. A large radius saves mass, but the rim speed limits how large it can be.

Problem 2.8 Motor and flywheel for a punching press

A press punches 30 holes a minute, each 25 mm in diameter in 20 mm plate with an ultimate shear stress of 300 MPa. The crankshaft turns once per hole, and punching takes one tenth of each turn. The punch force falls linearly from its peak to zero through the plate. The flywheel runs at a mean 250 rpm with K=0.1K = 0.1K=0.1. Find the motor power and the flywheel inertia.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Holes per minute30
Hole diameterddd25 mm
Plate thicknessttt20 mm
Ultimate shear stressτ\tauτ300 MPa
Punching time1/10 of each cycle
Flywheel speedNNN250 rpm
Coefficient of fluctuationKKK0.1

Find

  • Motor power
  • Flywheel moment of inertia III

Terms used in this problem

Sheared area
the cylinder the punch cuts out, circumference times thickness, πdt\pi d tπdt.
Ultimate shear stress τ\tauτ
the stress at which the plate shears through.
Energy per hole
area under the force-travel graph; a triangle here, so half the peak force times the thickness.
Role of the flywheel
the motor works steadily all cycle; the flywheel stores that energy and releases most of it in the short punching time.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the peak punching force
    P=πdtτ=π×0.025×0.020×300×106=471 kNP = \pi d t \tau = \pi \times 0.025 \times 0.020 \times 300 \times 10^6 = 471\ \text{kN}P=πdtτ=π×0.025×0.020×300×106=471 kN
  2. Step 2Find the energy per hole
    E=12×471 000×0.020=4712 JE = \tfrac12 \times 471\,000 \times 0.020 = 4712\ \text{J}E=21​×471000×0.020=4712 J
  3. Step 3Find the motor power

    The motor supplies this energy once every 2 s.

    Pm=4712×3060=2356 WP_m = 4712 \times \frac{30}{60} = 2356\ \text{W}Pm​=4712×6030​=2356 W
  4. Step 4Find the energy the flywheel must supply

    During punching (1/10 of the cycle) the motor gives 1/10 of EEE; the flywheel gives the rest.

    e=4712 (1−0.1)=4241 Je = 4712\,(1 - 0.1) = 4241\ \text{J}e=4712(1−0.1)=4241 J
  5. Step 5Find the flywheel inertia
    ω=2π×25060=26.18 rad/s,I=eKω2=42410.1×26.182=61.9 kg m2\omega = \frac{2\pi \times 250}{60} = 26.18\ \text{rad/s},\qquad I = \frac{e}{K\omega^2} = \frac{4241}{0.1 \times 26.18^2} = 61.9\ \text{kg m}^2ω=602π×250​=26.18 rad/s,I=Kω2e​=0.1×26.1824241​=61.9 kg m2

Answer Motor about 2.4 kW; I=61.9I = 61.9I=61.9 kg m² (for example a 248 kg rim at 0.5 m mean radius).

Without a flywheel the motor would have to give 4712 J in 0.2 s, about 24 kW.

Short problems

2.AA link of mass 4 kg has an acceleration of its mass centre of 25 m/s² to the right. Find its inertia force.

Term: Inertia force: equal and opposite to maGm a_GmaG​.

    Fi=−maG=−4×25=−100 NF_i = -m a_G = -4 \times 25 = -100\ \text{N}Fi​=−maG​=−4×25=−100 N

Answer 100 N to the left, acting through GGG.

2.BA rod has kG=0.12k_G = 0.12kG​=0.12 m. One equivalent mass sits 0.20 m from GGG. Where must the other be for a dynamically equivalent two-mass system?

Answer 0.072 m on the other side of GGG.

2.CThe maximum fluctuation of energy is 5 kJ at a mean speed of 30 rad/s, and KKK must not exceed 2%. Find the moment of inertia needed.

Answer I=278I = 278I=278 kg m².

2.DFind the safe rim speed of a cast-iron flywheel with ρ=7200\rho = 7200ρ=7200 kg/m³ and safe stress 7.2 MPa.

Term: Hoop stress: tension around the spinning rim.

  1. Step 1Use σ=ρv2\sigma = \rho v^2σ=ρv2
    v=7.2×1067200=1000=31.6 m/sv = \sqrt{\frac{7.2 \times 10^6}{7200}} = \sqrt{1000} = 31.6\ \text{m/s}v=72007.2×106​​=1000​=31.6 m/s

Problem 3.1 Natural frequency from static deflection

A 40 kg motor settles 12 mm on its spring mounts. Find its natural frequency of vertical vibration.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Massmmm40 kg
Static deflectionΔ\DeltaΔ12 mm = 0.012 m

Find

  • Natural frequency fnf_nfn​, period and total stiffness

Terms used in this problem

Static deflection Δ\DeltaΔ
how far the springs compress under the weight alone.
Stiffness sss
force per unit deflection of the springs, in N/m; at rest sΔ=mgs\Delta = mgsΔ=mg.
Natural frequency
the frequency at which the system vibrates by itself once disturbed: ωn\omega_nωn​ in rad/s or fn=ωn/2πf_n = \omega_n/2\pifn​=ωn​/2π in Hz (cycles per second).
Period
the time for one cycle, 1/fn1/f_n1/fn​.

Solution

  1. Step 1Relate stiffness to deflection

    At rest the spring force holds the weight, so s/m=g/Δs/m = g/\Deltas/m=g/Δ.

    ωn=sm=gΔ\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{s}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\Delta}}ωn​=ms​​=Δg​​
  2. Step 2Find the natural frequency
    ωn=9.810.012=28.6 rad/s,fn=28.62π=4.55 Hz\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{9.81}{0.012}} = 28.6\ \text{rad/s},\qquad f_n = \frac{28.6}{2\pi} = 4.55\ \text{Hz}ωn​=0.0129.81​​=28.6 rad/s,fn​=2π28.6​=4.55 Hz
  3. Step 3Find the period and stiffness
    tp=14.55=0.22 s,s=mgΔ=40×9.810.012=32.7 kN/mt_p = \frac{1}{4.55} = 0.22\ \text{s},\qquad s = \frac{mg}{\Delta} = \frac{40 \times 9.81}{0.012} = 32.7\ \text{kN/m}tp​=4.551​=0.22 s,s=Δmg​=0.01240×9.81​=32.7 kN/m

Answer fn=4.55f_n = 4.55fn​=4.55 Hz.

Once Δ\DeltaΔ is known the mass is not needed for the frequency.

Problem 3.2 Effect of the spring mass, and amplitude from starting conditions

A 5 kg mass hangs on a spring of stiffness 2 kN/m whose own mass is 0.9 kg. Find the natural frequency with and without the spring mass. Then the mass is given 10 mm displacement and 0.3 m/s velocity at t=0t = 0t=0; find the amplitude (ignore the spring mass).

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Massmmm5 kg
Stiffnesssss2000 N/m
Spring massm1m_1m1​0.9 kg
Starting displacementx0x_0x0​0.010 m
Starting velocityv0v_0v0​0.3 m/s

Find

  • fnf_nfn​ with and without the spring mass
  • Amplitude XXX

Terms used in this problem

Spring mass correction
the coils move too, slower near the fixed end; by the energy method one third of the spring mass adds to mmm.
Amplitude XXX
the greatest displacement from the rest position in the vibration.
Initial conditions
the displacement and velocity at t=0t = 0t=0; together they set the amplitude.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find fnf_nfn​ without the spring mass
    fn=12π20005=202π=3.18 Hzf_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{2000}{5}} = \frac{20}{2\pi} = 3.18\ \text{Hz}fn​=2π1​52000​​=2π20​=3.18 Hz
  2. Step 2Find fnf_nfn​ with the spring mass
    m+m13=5+0.3=5.3 kg,fn=12π20005.3=3.09 Hzm + \frac{m_1}{3} = 5 + 0.3 = 5.3\ \text{kg},\qquad f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{2000}{5.3}} = 3.09\ \text{Hz}m+3m1​​=5+0.3=5.3 kg,fn​=2π1​5.32000​​=3.09 Hz
  3. Step 3Find the amplitude

    Free vibration is x=Xsin⁡(ωnt+ϕ)x = X\sin(\omega_n t + \phi)x=Xsin(ωn​t+ϕ); the two starting values combine as legs of a right triangle.

    X=x02+(v0ωn)2=0.0102+(0.320)2=0.018 mX = \sqrt{x_0^2 + \left(\frac{v_0}{\omega_n}\right)^2} = \sqrt{0.010^2 + \left(\frac{0.3}{20}\right)^2} = 0.018\ \text{m}X=x02​+(ωn​v0​​)2​=0.0102+(200.3​)2​=0.018 m

Answer 3.18 Hz without and 3.09 Hz with the spring mass (about 3% lower); amplitude 18 mm.

Problem 3.3 Damping from a decay record

A 10 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 4 kN/m is displaced and released. The amplitude falls from 20 mm to 5 mm in 4 cycles. Find the logarithmic decrement, the damping ratio and the damping coefficient.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue

Terms used in this problem

Solution

  2. Step 2Find the damping ratio

  3. Step 3Find critical and actual damping
    cc=2sm=24000×10=400 N s/m,c=ξcc=0.055×400=22.0 N s/mc_c = 2\sqrt{sm} = 2\sqrt{4000 \times 10} = 400\ \text{N s/m},\qquad c = \xi c_c = 0.055 \times 400 = 22.0\ \text{N s/m}cc​=2sm​=24000×10​=400 N s/m,c=ξcc​=0.055×400=22.0 N s/m
  4. Step 4Find the frequencies
    ωn=4000/10=20 rad/s,ωd=201−0.0552=19.97 rad/s\omega_n = \sqrt{4000/10} = 20\ \text{rad/s},\qquad \omega_d = 20\sqrt{1 - 0.055^2} = 19.97\ \text{rad/s}ωn​=4000/10​=20 rad/s,ωd​=201−0.0552​=19.97 rad/s

Answer δ=0.347\delta = 0.347δ=0.347, ξ=0.055\xi = 0.055ξ=0.055, c=22.0c = 22.0c=22.0 N s/m.

Problem 3.4 Steady-state amplitude and phase of forced vibration

A 20 kg mass on a spring of 8 kN/m with a damper of 200 N s/m is driven by a force F=100sin⁡15tF = 100\sin 15tF=100sin15t N. Find the steady amplitude and the phase lag.

  4. Step 4Find the amplitude

  5. Step 5Find the phase lag

Answer A=21.7A = 21.7A=21.7 mm, lagging the force by 40.6°.

Problem 3.5 Spring mounts to isolate a pump set

A 150 kg pump set runs at 1450 rpm. It is to sit on four equal springs so that only 10% of its out-of-balance force reaches the floor. Neglecting damping, find the stiffness of each spring and the static deflection. Then find the transmissibility if the mounts give ξ=0.05\xi = 0.05ξ=0.05.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Massmmm150 kg
SpeedNNN1450 rpm
Allowed transmissibilityε\varepsilonε0.10
Number of springs4
Damping ratio (check)ξ\xiξ0.05

Find

  • Stiffness of each spring
  • Static deflection
  • ε\varepsilonε with damping

Terms used in this problem

Out-of-balance force
the rotating force from an unbalanced rotor; it acts at the running speed.
Transmissibility ε\varepsilonε
force reaching the floor divided by the force applied.
Isolation
achieved only when r=ω/ωn>2r = \omega/\omega_n > \sqrt2r=ω/ωn​>2​; soft mounts make ωn\omega_nωn​ low.
Springs in parallel
four springs under one machine add their stiffnesses.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the running speed in rad/s
    ω=2π×145060=151.8 rad/s\omega = \frac{2\pi \times 1450}{60} = 151.8\ \text{rad/s}ω=602π×1450​=151.8 rad/s
  2. Step 2Find the frequency ratio needed

    Undamped, above resonance, ε=1/(r2−1)\varepsilon = 1/(r^2 - 1)ε=1/(r2−1).

    r2=1+1ε=11,r=3.317r^2 = 1 + \frac{1}{\varepsilon} = 11,\qquad r = 3.317r2=1+ε1​=11,r=3.317
  3. Step 3Find the natural frequency
    ωn=ωr=151.83.317=45.8 rad/s (7.29 Hz)\omega_n = \frac{\omega}{r} = \frac{151.8}{3.317} = 45.8\ \text{rad/s}\ (7.29\ \text{Hz})ωn​=rω​=3.317151.8​=45.8 rad/s (7.29 Hz)

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the stiffness
    s=mωn2=150×45.82=314.4 kN/m,each spring 78.6 kN/ms = m\omega_n^2 = 150 \times 45.8^2 = 314.4\ \text{kN/m},\qquad \text{each spring } 78.6\ \text{kN/m}s=mωn2​=150×45.82=314.4 kN/m,each spring 78.6 kN/m
  2. Step 5Find the static deflection
    Δ=gωn2=9.8145.82=4.7 mm\Delta = \frac{g}{\omega_n^2} = \frac{9.81}{45.8^2} = 4.7\ \text{mm}Δ=ωn2​g​=45.829.81​=4.7 mm
  3. Step 6Check with damping
    ε=1+(2ξr)2(1−r2)2+(2ξr)2=1+0.3322102+0.3322=0.105\varepsilon = \frac{\sqrt{1 + (2\xi r)^2}}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\xi r)^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 0.332^2}}{\sqrt{10^2 + 0.332^2}} = 0.105ε=(1−r2)2+(2ξr)2​1+(2ξr)2​​=102+0.3322​1+0.3322​​=0.105

Answer Each spring about 78.6 kN/m, static deflection 4.7 mm; with ξ=0.05\xi = 0.05ξ=0.05, ε=0.105\varepsilon = 0.105ε=0.105.

Damping makes isolation slightly worse above r=2r = \sqrt2r=2​, though it helps when passing through resonance at start-up.

Problem 3.6 Vehicle body on a wavy road (base excitation)

A pick-up body sits on its springs with natural frequency 1.29 Hz (ωn=8.09\omega_n = 8.09ωn​=8.09 rad/s) and ξ=0.3\xi = 0.3ξ=0.3. A murram road has smooth waves of amplitude 25 mm every 5 m. Find the body amplitude at 30 km/h, and the speed at which the body bounces most.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue

    v=303.6=8.33 m/s,f=8.335=1.67 Hz,ω=10.5 rad/sv = \frac{30}{3.6} = 8.33\ \text{m/s},\qquad f = \frac{8.33}{5} = 1.67\ \text{Hz},\qquad \omega = 10.5\ \text{rad/s}v=3.630​=8.33 m/s,f=58.33​=1.67 Hz,ω=10.5 rad/s
  2. Step 2Find the frequency ratio

  3. Step 3Find the amplitude ratio
    AY=1+(2ξr)2(1−r2)2+(2ξr)2=1+0.7820.692+0.782=1.271.03=1.23\frac{A}{Y} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + (2\xi r)^2}}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\xi r)^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 0.78^2}}{\sqrt{0.69^2 + 0.78^2}} = \frac{1.27}{1.03} = 1.23YA​=(1−r2)2+(2ξr)2​1+(2ξr)2​​=0.692+0.782​1+0.782​​=1.031.27​=1.23

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the body amplitude
    A=1.23×25=31 mmA = 1.23 \times 25 = 31\ \text{mm}A=1.23×25=31 mm
  2. Step 5Find the speed of worst bouncing

    Near resonance, r=1r = 1r=1:

    AY=1+0.620.6=1.94,A=49 mm\frac{A}{Y} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 0.6^2}}{0.6} = 1.94,\qquad A = 49\ \text{mm}YA​=0.61+0.62​​=1.94,A=49 mm

Above about 33 km/h (r>2r > \sqrt2r>2​) the body moves less than the road.

Problem 4.1 Effort and efficiency of a screw jack

A screw jack has a single-start square thread of mean diameter 50 mm and pitch 10 mm, with μ=0.12\mu = 0.12μ=0.12. It lifts 20 kN. The load cup is a collar of mean radius 30 mm with μc=0.15\mu_c = 0.15μc​=0.15. The lever is 0.5 m long. Find the effort to raise and to lower the load, and the efficiency.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Mean thread diameterddd50 mm
Pitch (single start, so lead)lll10 mm
Thread frictionμ\muμ0.12
LoadWWW20 kN
Collar mean radiusRcR_cRc​30 mm
Collar frictionμc\mu_cμc​0.15
Lever length0.5 m

Find

  • Torque and effort to raise and to lower
  • Efficiency

Terms used in this problem

Pitch and lead
pitch is the distance between threads; lead is how far the screw advances in one turn (pitch times number of starts).
Helix angle α\alphaα
the slope of the thread: unwrapped, one turn is a ramp of rise lll over run πd\pi dπd.
Friction angle ϕ\phiϕ
tan⁡ϕ=μ\tan\phi = \mutanϕ=μ; friction tilts the reaction by this angle.
Collar
the flat bearing under the load cup; it adds its own friction torque.
Self-locking
the load will not run down by itself, which happens when ϕ>α\phi > \alphaϕ>α.
Efficiency
useful work (lifting) over work put in at the lever.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the helix and friction angles
    tan⁡α=lπd=10π×50,α=3.64∘;ϕ=tan⁡−10.12=6.84∘\tan\alpha = \frac{l}{\pi d} = \frac{10}{\pi \times 50},\quad \alpha = 3.64^\circ;\qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}0.12 = 6.84^\circtanα=πdl​=π×5010​,α=3.64∘;ϕ=tan−10.12=6.84∘
  2. Step 2Check self-locking

    ϕ>α\phi > \alphaϕ>α, so the jack holds the load without effort.

  3. Step 3Find the torque to raise

    Thread torque plus collar torque, with r=d/2r = d/2r=d/2.

    Tth=Wrtan⁡(α+ϕ)=20 000×0.025×tan⁡10.49∘=92.5 N mT_{th} = W r\tan(\alpha + \phi) = 20\,000 \times 0.025 \times \tan 10.49^\circ = 92.5\ \text{N m}Tth​=Wrtan(α+ϕ)=20000×0.025×tan10.49∘=92.5 N m
    Tc=μcWRc=0.15×20 000×0.03=90 N m,T=182.5 N mT_c = \mu_c W R_c = 0.15 \times 20\,000 \times 0.03 = 90\ \text{N m},\qquad T = 182.5\ \text{N m}Tc​=μc​WRc​=0.15×20000×0.03=90 N m,T=182.5 N m
  4. Step 4Find the effort at the lever
    P=182.50.5=365 NP = \frac{182.5}{0.5} = 365\ \text{N}P=0.5182.5​=365 N

Solution, continued

  1. Step 5Find the torque and effort to lower
    T=Wrtan⁡(ϕ−α)+μcWRc=28.0+90=118 N m,P=236 NT = W r\tan(\phi - \alpha) + \mu_c W R_c = 28.0 + 90 = 118\ \text{N m},\qquad P = 236\ \text{N}T=Wrtan(ϕ−α)+μc​WRc​=28.0+90=118 N m,P=236 N
  2. Step 6Find the efficiency

    Work per turn: lifting WlWlWl against effort 2πT2\pi T2πT.

    η=Wl2πT=20 000×0.012π×182.5=17.4%\eta = \frac{W l}{2\pi T} = \frac{20\,000 \times 0.01}{2\pi \times 182.5} = 17.4\%η=2πTWl​=2π×182.520000×0.01​=17.4%
    thread alone: tan⁡αtan⁡(α+ϕ)=34.4%\text{thread alone: } \frac{\tan\alpha}{\tan(\alpha + \phi)} = 34.4\%thread alone: tan(α+ϕ)tanα​=34.4%

Answer Raise: 182.5 N m, 365 N at the lever. Lower: 118 N m, 236 N. Efficiency 17.4% (34.4% for the thread alone).

Collar friction halves the efficiency, which is why good jacks put a thrust ball bearing under the cup.

Problem 4.2 Power lost in a flat collar

A flat collar of 300 mm outside and 200 mm inside diameter carries an axial thrust of 40 kN on a shaft turning at 150 rpm, with μ=0.04\mu = 0.04μ=0.04. Find the power lost in friction by both theories.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Outside radiusRoR_oRo​0.15 m
Inside radiusRiR_iRi​0.10 m
Axial thrustFFF40 kN
SpeedNNN150 rpm
Friction coefficientμ\muμ0.04

Find

  • Friction torque and power lost, uniform pressure and uniform wear

Terms used in this problem

Collar bearing
a ring-shaped face that takes an axial (end) thrust on a turning shaft.
Uniform pressure theory
pressure the same over the whole face; fits a new bearing and gives the larger torque.
Uniform wear theory
wear the same everywhere, so pressure × radius is constant; fits a worn-in bearing.
Power lost
friction torque times angular speed, all turned into heat.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the torque, uniform pressure
    T=23μFRo3−Ri3Ro2−Ri2=23×0.04×40 000×0.0023750.0125=202.7 N mT = \tfrac23\mu F\frac{R_o^3 - R_i^3}{R_o^2 - R_i^2} = \tfrac23 \times 0.04 \times 40\,000 \times \frac{0.002375}{0.0125} = 202.7\ \text{N m}T=32​μFRo2​−Ri2​Ro3​−Ri3​​=32​×0.04×40000×0.01250.002375​=202.7 N m
  2. Step 2Find the torque, uniform wear
    T=12μF(Ro+Ri)=12×0.04×40 000×0.25=200 N mT = \tfrac12\mu F(R_o + R_i) = \tfrac12 \times 0.04 \times 40\,000 \times 0.25 = 200\ \text{N m}T=21​μF(Ro​+Ri​)=21​×0.04×40000×0.25=200 N m
  3. Step 3Find the shaft speed
    ω=2π×15060=15.71 rad/s\omega = \frac{2\pi \times 150}{60} = 15.71\ \text{rad/s}ω=602π×150​=15.71 rad/s
  4. Step 4Find the power lost
    P=Tω:202.7×15.71=3.18 kW,200×15.71=3.14 kWP = T\omega:\qquad 202.7 \times 15.71 = 3.18\ \text{kW},\qquad 200 \times 15.71 = 3.14\ \text{kW}P=Tω:202.7×15.71=3.18 kW,200×15.71=3.14 kW

Answer 3.18 kW by uniform pressure (use this for the bearing) and 3.14 kW by uniform wear.

Problem 4.3 Single-plate clutch of a minibus

A single-plate clutch has linings of 250 mm outside and 150 mm inside diameter, both faces working, μ=0.3\mu = 0.3μ=0.3 and a clamp force of 4 kN. Find the torque capacity by both theories, the power it can pass at 3000 rpm, and the greatest lining pressure under uniform wear.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Outside radiusRoR_oRo​0.125 m
Inside radiusRiR_iRi​0.075 m

Terms used in this problem

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the torque, uniform wear

    The design value: it is the lower, safe one.

    T=nμFRo+Ri2=2×0.3×4000×0.1=240 N mT = n\mu F\frac{R_o + R_i}{2} = 2 \times 0.3 \times 4000 \times 0.1 = 240\ \text{N m}T=nμF2Ro​+Ri​​=2×0.3×4000×0.1=240 N m
  2. Step 2Find the torque, uniform pressure
    Rm=23Ro3−Ri3Ro2−Ri2=102.1 mm,T=nμFRm=245 N mR_m = \tfrac23\frac{R_o^3 - R_i^3}{R_o^2 - R_i^2} = 102.1\ \text{mm},\qquad T = n\mu F R_m = 245\ \text{N m}Rm​=32​Ro2​−Ri2​Ro3​−Ri3​​=102.1 mm,T=nμFRm​=245 N m
  3. Step 3Find the power
    P=Tω=240×2π×300060=75.4 kWP = T\omega = 240 \times \frac{2\pi \times 3000}{60} = 75.4\ \text{kW}P=Tω=240×602π×3000​=75.4 kW
  4. Step 4Find the greatest pressure

    With pr=Cpr = Cpr=C, the force is F=2πC(Ro−Ri)F = 2\pi C(R_o - R_i)F=2πC(Ro​−Ri​), and pmax=C/Rip_{max} = C/R_ipmax​=C/Ri​.

    pmax=F2πRi(Ro−Ri)=40002π×0.075×0.05=170 kPap_{max} = \frac{F}{2\pi R_i(R_o - R_i)} = \frac{4000}{2\pi \times 0.075 \times 0.05} = 170\ \text{kPa}pmax​=2πRi​(Ro​−Ri​)F​=2π×0.075×0.054000​=170 kPa

Answer 240 N m (uniform wear) and 245 N m (uniform pressure); 75.4 kW at 3000 rpm; 170 kPa at the inner edge.

Problem 4.4 Centrifugal clutch

A centrifugal clutch has four shoes of 1.5 kg each, with mass centres 120 mm from the axis. The drum inner radius is 150 mm and μ=0.25\mu = 0.25μ=0.25. The shoes start to touch the drum at 500 rpm. Find the spring force per shoe, and the torque and power at 1000 rpm.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Shoes4
Shoe massmmm1.5 kg
Radius of shoe mass centrerrr0.12 m
Drum radiusRRR0.15 m
Friction coefficientμ\muμ0.25
Engagement speed500 rpm
Running speed1000 rpm

Find

  • Spring force per shoe
  • Torque and power at 1000 rpm

Terms used in this problem

Shoe
a weighted pad that flies outwards as the shaft spins.
Drum
the outer cylinder the shoes press on; it drives the load.
Centrifugal force
mrω2m r \omega^2mrω2, the outward pull on a shoe turning at ω\omegaω.
Engagement speed ω′\omega'ω′
the speed at which the centrifugal force just equals the spring pull, so the shoes start to touch.

Solution

  1. Step 1Convert the speeds
    ω′=2π×50060=52.4 rad/s,ω=2π×100060=104.7 rad/s\omega' = \frac{2\pi \times 500}{60} = 52.4\ \text{rad/s},\qquad \omega = \frac{2\pi \times 1000}{60} = 104.7\ \text{rad/s}ω′=602π×500​=52.4 rad/s,ω=602π×1000​=104.7 rad/s
  2. Step 2Find the spring force

    At engagement the spring just holds the shoe.

    S=mrω′2=1.5×0.12×52.42=493 NS = m r\omega'^2 = 1.5 \times 0.12 \times 52.4^2 = 493\ \text{N}S=mrω′2=1.5×0.12×52.42=493 N
  3. Step 3Find the net force on the drum per shoe
    N=mr(ω2−ω′2)=0.18×(10 966−2742)=1480 NN = m r(\omega^2 - \omega'^2) = 0.18 \times (10\,966 - 2742) = 1480\ \text{N}N=mr(ω2−ω′2)=0.18×(10966−2742)=1480 N
  4. Step 4Find the torque and power

    Each shoe gives friction μN\mu NμN at the drum radius.

    T=4×0.25×1480×0.15=222 N m,P=222×104.7=23.3 kWT = 4 \times 0.25 \times 1480 \times 0.15 = 222\ \text{N m},\qquad P = 222 \times 104.7 = 23.3\ \text{kW}T=4×0.25×1480×0.15=222 N m,P=222×104.7=23.3 kW

Answer 493 N per shoe; 222 N m and 23.3 kW at 1000 rpm.

The torque grows with ω2−ω′2\omega^2 - \omega'^2ω2−ω′2, so it climbs steeply once the shoes engage.

Problem 4.5 Friction loss in a journal bearing

A journal of 100 mm diameter carries 25 kN at 300 rpm under boundary lubrication, μ=0.05\mu = 0.05μ=0.05. Find the friction-circle radius, the friction torque and the power lost.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Journal radiusrrr50 mm
LoadWWW25 kN
SpeedNNN300 rpm
Friction coefficientμ\muμ0.05

Find

  • Friction-circle radius
  • Friction torque
  • Power lost

Terms used in this problem

Journal
the part of a shaft that turns inside a bearing.
Boundary lubrication
only a thin film of grease or oil, so metal partly touches and μ\muμ is fairly high.
Friction circle
a small circle of radius rsin⁡ϕr\sin\phirsinϕ about the shaft centre; the bearing reaction always touches it.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the friction angle
    ϕ=tan⁡−10.05=2.86∘\phi = \tan^{-1}0.05 = 2.86^\circϕ=tan−10.05=2.86∘
  2. Step 2Find the friction-circle radius
    rf=rsin⁡ϕ=50×0.04994=2.50 mmr_f = r\sin\phi = 50 \times 0.04994 = 2.50\ \text{mm}rf​=rsinϕ=50×0.04994=2.50 mm
  3. Step 3Find the friction torque

    The reaction WWW acts at arm rfr_frf​.

    Tf=Wrf=25 000×0.002497=62.4 N mT_f = W r_f = 25\,000 \times 0.002497 = 62.4\ \text{N m}Tf​=Wrf​=25000×0.002497=62.4 N m
  4. Step 4Find the power lost
    ω=31.4 rad/s,P=62.4×31.4=1.96 kW\omega = 31.4\ \text{rad/s},\qquad P = 62.4 \times 31.4 = 1.96\ \text{kW}ω=31.4 rad/s,P=62.4×31.4=1.96 kW

Answer 2.50 mm; 62.4 N m; 1.96 kW, all of it heat in the bearing.

A full oil film (μ\muμ about 0.005) would cut this loss tenfold.

Short problems

4.AA block just starts to slide when the plane is tilted to 16.7°. Find the coefficient of friction.

Term: Angle of repose: the steepest slope on which the block stays put.

    μ=tan⁡16.7∘=0.30\mu = \tan 16.7^\circ = 0.30μ=tan16.7∘=0.30

Answer μ=0.30\mu = 0.30μ=0.30.

4.BA multi-plate clutch has 4 driving plates and 3 driven plates. How many pairs of friction surfaces are there?

  1. Step 1Count the faces in contact
    n=n1+n2−1=4+3−1=6n = n_1 + n_2 - 1 = 4 + 3 - 1 = 6n=n1​+n2​−1=4+3−1=6

Answer 6.

4.CA conical pivot of semi-angle 30° replaces a flat pivot of the same radius and load. How does the friction torque change?

Term: Semi-angle: half the cone angle.

  1. Step 1Divide by sin⁡α\sin\alphasinα
    TconeTflat=1sin⁡30∘=2\frac{T_{cone}}{T_{flat}} = \frac{1}{\sin 30^\circ} = 2Tflat​Tcone​​=sin30∘1​=2

Answer It doubles.

Problem 5.1 Teeth and base circle from the centre distance

Two gears mesh with a velocity ratio of 1/3, module 4 mm, pressure angle 20° and centre distance 200 mm. Find the numbers of teeth and the base-circle radius of the wheel.

Rattan (2009), Example 10.3

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Velocity ratio1/3, so T2=3T1T_2 = 3T_1T2​=3T1​
Modulemmm4 mm
Pressure angleϕ\phiϕ20°
Centre distanceCCC200 mm

Find

  • Teeth T1T_1T1​ (pinion) and T2T_2T2​ (wheel)
  • Base-circle radius of the wheel

Terms used in this problem

Module mmm
pitch diameter divided by number of teeth, m=d/Tm = d/Tm=d/T, in mm. Gears that mesh have the same module.
Pitch circle
the imaginary circle on which two meshing gears roll without slipping; its diameter is d=mTd = mTd=mT.
Pressure angle ϕ\phiϕ
the angle between the line along which the teeth push (line of action) and the common tangent of the pitch circles; usually 20°.
Pinion and wheel
the smaller and the larger gear of a pair.
Centre distance CCC
distance between the gear axes, the sum of the pitch radii.
Base circle
the circle from which the involute tooth curve is unwound; its radius is rcos⁡ϕr\cos\phircosϕ.

Solution

  1. Step 1Write the centre distance
    C=m(T1+T2)2C = \frac{m(T_1 + T_2)}{2}C=2m(T1​+T2​)​
  2. Step 2Put in the ratio and solve
    200=4(T1+3T1)2=8T1,T1=25,T2=75200 = \frac{4(T_1 + 3T_1)}{2} = 8T_1,\qquad T_1 = 25,\quad T_2 = 75200=24(T1​+3T1​)​=8T1​,T1​=25,T2​=75
  3. Step 3Find the wheel pitch radius
    d2=mT2=4×75=300 mm,R=150 mmd_2 = mT_2 = 4 \times 75 = 300\ \text{mm},\qquad R = 150\ \text{mm}d2​=mT2​=4×75=300 mm,R=150 mm
  4. Step 4Find the base-circle radius
    Rb=Rcos⁡ϕ=150cos⁡20∘=141 mmR_b = R\cos\phi = 150\cos 20^\circ = 141\ \text{mm}Rb​=Rcosϕ=150cos20∘=141 mm

Answer 25 and 75 teeth; base-circle radius of the wheel 141 mm.

Problem 5.2 Path of contact, angle of action and sliding

Two 20° involute gears have a gear ratio of 3. The pinion has 24 teeth of module 6 mm, and the addendum is one module. The pitch-line velocity is 1.5 m/s. Find the path of contact, contact ratio, angle of action of the pinion and the greatest velocity of sliding.

Rattan (2009), Example 10.5

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Pinion teethttt24
Wheel teethTTT72
Modulemmm6 mm
Pressure angleϕ\phiϕ20°
Addendumaaa6 mm
Pitch-line velocityvvv1.5 m/s

Find

  • Path of contact, contact ratio, angle of action, greatest sliding velocity

Terms used in this problem

Addendum
the height of a tooth above the pitch circle; the addendum circle has radius r+ar + ar+a.
Path of contact
the length of the line of action on which the teeth touch: approach (KPKPKP, before the pitch point) plus recess (PLPLPL, after).
Arc of contact
the distance the pitch circle turns while one pair of teeth is in contact: path over cos⁡ϕ\cos\phicosϕ.
Contact ratio
arc of contact over circular pitch πm\pi mπm: the average number of tooth pairs in mesh.
Angle of action
the angle the pinion turns through while one pair is in contact.
Sliding velocity
how fast the tooth faces rub; zero at the pitch point PPP, largest at the ends of contact.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the pitch radii
    r=6×242=72 mm,R=6×722=216 mmr = \frac{6 \times 24}{2} = 72\ \text{mm},\qquad R = \frac{6 \times 72}{2} = 216\ \text{mm}r=26×24​=72 mm,R=26×72​=216 mm
  2. Step 2Find the path of approach

    Set by the wheel addendum.

    KP=(R+a)2−R2cos⁡2ϕ−Rsin⁡ϕ=2222−203.02−73.9=16.04 mmKP = \sqrt{(R + a)^2 - R^2\cos^2\phi} - R\sin\phi = \sqrt{222^2 - 203.0^2} - 73.9 = 16.04\ \text{mm}KP=(R+a)2−R2cos2ϕ​−Rsinϕ=2222−203.02​−73.9=16.04 mm
  3. Step 3Find the path of recess

    Set by the pinion addendum.

    PL=(r+a)2−r2cos⁡2ϕ−rsin⁡ϕ=782−67.72−24.6=14.19 mmPL = \sqrt{(r + a)^2 - r^2\cos^2\phi} - r\sin\phi = \sqrt{78^2 - 67.7^2} - 24.6 = 14.19\ \text{mm}PL=(r+a)2−r2cos2ϕ​−rsinϕ=782−67.72​−24.6=14.19 mm

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the path, arc and contact ratio
    KL=30.23 mm,arc=30.23cos⁡20∘=32.17 mm,32.17π×6=1.71KL = 30.23\ \text{mm},\qquad \text{arc} = \frac{30.23}{\cos 20^\circ} = 32.17\ \text{mm},\qquad \frac{32.17}{\pi \times 6} = 1.71KL=30.23 mm,arc=cos20∘30.23​=32.17 mm,π×632.17​=1.71
  2. Step 5Find the angle of action of the pinion
    δ=32.1772=0.447 rad=25.6∘\delta = \frac{32.17}{72} = 0.447\ \text{rad} = 25.6^\circδ=7232.17​=0.447 rad=25.6∘
  3. Step 6Find the greatest sliding velocity

    At the end of the longer path (approach).

    ω1=1.50.072=20.83,ω2=20.833=6.94 rad/s\omega_1 = \frac{1.5}{0.072} = 20.83,\quad \omega_2 = \frac{20.83}{3} = 6.94\ \text{rad/s}ω1​=0.0721.5​=20.83,ω2​=320.83​=6.94 rad/s
    vs=(ω1+ω2)×KP=27.78×0.01604=0.446 m/sv_s = (\omega_1 + \omega_2) \times KP = 27.78 \times 0.01604 = 0.446\ \text{m/s}vs​=(ω1​+ω2​)×KP=27.78×0.01604=0.446 m/s

Answer Path of contact 30.2 mm, contact ratio 1.71, angle of action 25.6°, greatest sliding 0.446 m/s at the start of contact.

Problem 5.3 Checking for interference

Two 20° involute spur gears have module 10 mm and addendum one module. The wheel has 40 teeth and the pinion 20. Will the gears interfere?

Rattan (2009), Example 10.10

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Modulemmm10 mm
Addendumaaa10 mm
Wheel teethTTT40
Pinion teethttt20
Pressure angleϕ\phiϕ20°

Find

  • Whether either gear interferes

Terms used in this problem

Interference
the tip of one tooth digging into the root of the other, below the base circle where there is no involute.
Interference point
the point where the line of action touches the other gear's base circle; contact must not go beyond it.
Largest addendum radius
the biggest tip radius that keeps contact inside the interference point.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the radii
    R=200 mm,r=100 mm,Ra=210 mm,ra=110 mm,C=300 mmR = 200\ \text{mm},\quad r = 100\ \text{mm},\quad R_a = 210\ \text{mm},\quad r_a = 110\ \text{mm},\quad C = 300\ \text{mm}R=200 mm,r=100 mm,Ra​=210 mm,ra​=110 mm,C=300 mm
  2. Step 2Find the largest wheel addendum radius

    The wheel tip may reach the point where the line of action touches the pinion base circle.

    Ra,max=(Rcos⁡ϕ)2+(Csin⁡ϕ)2=187.92+102.62=214.1 mmR_{a,max} = \sqrt{(R\cos\phi)^2 + (C\sin\phi)^2} = \sqrt{187.9^2 + 102.6^2} = 214.1\ \text{mm}Ra,max​=(Rcosϕ)2+(Csinϕ)2​=187.92+102.62​=214.1 mm
  3. Step 3Compare for the wheel
    Ra=210<214.1 mm: no interferenceR_a = 210 < 214.1\ \text{mm}:\ \text{no interference}Ra​=210<214.1 mm: no interference
  4. Step 4Check the pinion the same way
    ra,max=(100cos⁡20∘)2+102.62=139.1 mm>110 mmr_{a,max} = \sqrt{(100\cos 20^\circ)^2 + 102.6^2} = 139.1\ \text{mm} > 110\ \text{mm}ra,max​=(100cos20∘)2+102.62​=139.1 mm>110 mm

Answer No interference: the wheel addendum could be up to 14.1 mm.

Problem 5.4 Fewest teeth for a 3 to 1 pair

Find the fewest teeth on a 20° full-depth pair with gear ratio 3 so that there is no interference.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Gear ratioGGG3
Pressure angleϕ\phiϕ20°
Addendum1 module (full depth)

Find

  • Fewest teeth on the wheel and the pinion

Terms used in this problem

Full depth
standard teeth with an addendum of one module.
Gear ratio GGG
wheel teeth over pinion teeth, T/tT/tT/t.
Minimum teeth
the fewest teeth for which the tip of the mating gear stays clear of the interference point.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the term under the root
    1G(1G+2)sin⁡2ϕ=13×73×0.1170=0.0910\frac{1}{G}\left(\frac{1}{G} + 2\right)\sin^2\phi = \frac13 \times \frac73 \times 0.1170 = 0.0910G1​(G1​+2)sin2ϕ=31​×37​×0.1170=0.0910
  2. Step 2Find the fewest wheel teeth
    Tmin=21+0.0910−1=20.04451=44.9, so 45T_{min} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 + 0.0910} - 1} = \frac{2}{0.04451} = 44.9,\ \text{so } 45Tmin​=1+0.0910​−12​=0.044512​=44.9, so 45
  3. Step 3Find the pinion teeth
    t=453=15t = \frac{45}{3} = 15t=345​=15

Answer Wheel 45 teeth, pinion 15 teeth.

Against a rack the pinion would need 2/sin⁡220∘=17.12/\sin^2 20^\circ = 17.12/sin220∘=17.1, so 18 teeth.

Problem 5.5 Reverted gear train for a maize mill

A 1440 rpm motor must drive a mill at about 120 rpm through a two-stage reverted train with the same module in both stages and no pinion below 20 teeth. Choose the teeth and find the output speed.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Motor speed1440 rpm
Target output120 rpm
Smallest pinion20 teeth

Find

  • Teeth on all four gears
  • Actual output speed

Terms used in this problem

Compound train
two gears fixed on one middle shaft, so the stage ratios multiply.
Reverted train
a compound train whose output shaft is in line with the input; both stages then have the same centre distance, so with one module T1+T2=T3+T4T_1 + T_2 = T_3 + T_4T1​+T2​=T3​+T4​.
Train value
output speed over input speed.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the overall ratio
    1440120=12\frac{1440}{120} = 121201440​=12
  2. Step 2Split it equally between stages
    12=3.46 per stage\sqrt{12} = 3.46\ \text{per stage}12​=3.46 per stage
  3. Step 3Choose the teeth

    With 20-tooth pinions the wheels need 20×3.46=69.320 \times 3.46 = 69.320×3.46=69.3; take 70.

    T1+T2=T3+T4=20+70=90T_1 + T_2 = T_3 + T_4 = 20 + 70 = 90T1​+T2​=T3​+T4​=20+70=90
  4. Step 4Find the output speed
    Nout=1440×2070×2070=117.6 rpmN_{out} = 1440 \times \frac{20}{70} \times \frac{20}{70} = 117.6\ \text{rpm}Nout​=1440×7020​×7020​=117.6 rpm

Answer 20/70 and 20/70; 117.6 rpm, 2% below the target, which a mill accepts.

Problem 5.6 Epicyclic train by the tabular method

An epicyclic train has an arm and two gears, A (30 teeth) and B (40 teeth). The arm turns about the centre of A at 80 rpm anticlockwise. Find the speed of B if (i) A is fixed, (ii) A turns at 240 rpm clockwise.

Rattan (2009), Example 11.3

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Teeth on ATAT_ATA​30
Teeth on BTBT_BTB​40
Arm speed80 rpm anticlockwise (+)
Case (ii) speed of A240 rpm clockwise (−)

Find

  • Speed of B in each case

Terms used in this problem

Epicyclic train
a train in which some gear axes (here B's) move round on an arm.
Arm (carrier)
the link that carries the moving gear round the fixed axis.
Tabular method
first fix the arm and turn one gear xxx turns; then turn everything together yyy turns; add the two.
Sign convention
anticlockwise positive; external gears in mesh turn opposite ways.

Solution

  1. Step 1Fix the arm and turn A by xxx

    B, in external mesh, turns the other way in the tooth ratio.

    Arm 0,A +x,B −3040x=−0.75x\text{Arm } 0,\qquad A\ {+x},\qquad B\ {-\tfrac{30}{40}x} = -0.75xArm 0,A +x,B −4030​x=−0.75x
  2. Step 2Add yyy to everything
    Arm y,A y+x,B y−0.75x\text{Arm } y,\qquad A\ y + x,\qquad B\ y - 0.75xArm y,A y+x,B y−0.75x
  3. Step 3Use the arm speed
    y=+80y = +80y=+80
  4. Step 4Case (i): A fixed
    y+x=0,x=−80,NB=80−0.75(−80)=140 rpmy + x = 0,\quad x = -80,\qquad N_B = 80 - 0.75(-80) = 140\ \text{rpm}y+x=0,x=−80,NB​=80−0.75(−80)=140 rpm
  5. Step 5Case (ii): A at 240 rpm clockwise
    y+x=−240,x=−320,NB=80+240=320 rpmy + x = -240,\quad x = -320,\qquad N_B = 80 + 240 = 320\ \text{rpm}y+x=−240,x=−320,NB​=80+240=320 rpm

Answer 140 rpm and 320 rpm, both anticlockwise.

Problem 5.7 Planetary reduction and its holding torque

A planetary stage has a 24-tooth sun and 36-tooth planets. The annulus is held. The sun is driven at 1500 rpm with 10 N m. Find the annulus teeth, the arm speed, the output torque and the torque needed to hold the annulus.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Sun teethTST_STS​24
Planet teethTPT_PTP​36
Annulusheld, NA=0N_A = 0NA​=0
Sun speed and torque1500 rpm, 10 N m

Find

  • Annulus teeth
  • Arm speed
  • Output and holding torques

Terms used in this problem

Sun, planets, annulus
the central gear, the gears that orbit it, and the internal-toothed outer ring.
Assembly condition
for equally spaced planets, (TS+TA)(T_S + T_A)(TS​+TA​) divided by the number of planets must be a whole number.
Power balance
with no losses the powers in and out add to zero: ∑Tω=0\sum T\omega = 0∑Tω=0.
Torque balance
the external torques on the whole gearbox add to zero: ∑T=0\sum T = 0∑T=0.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the annulus teeth

    The planets span the gap between sun and annulus.

    TA=TS+2TP=24+72=96,24+963=40 (three planets fit)T_A = T_S + 2T_P = 24 + 72 = 96,\qquad \frac{24 + 96}{3} = 40\ \text{(three planets fit)}TA​=TS​+2TP​=24+72=96,324+96​=40 (three planets fit)
  2. Step 2Find the arm speed

    Tabular method: arm fixed, sun +x+x+x gives annulus −x (24/96)-x\,(24/96)−x(24/96); adding yyy and setting the annulus to zero gives y=0.25xy = 0.25xy=0.25x and y+x=1500y + x = 1500y+x=1500.

    Narm=1500×TSTS+TA=1500×24120=300 rpmN_{arm} = 1500 \times \frac{T_S}{T_S + T_A} = 1500 \times \frac{24}{120} = 300\ \text{rpm}Narm​=1500×TS​+TA​TS​​=1500×12024​=300 rpm
  3. Step 3Find the output torque

    Power balance with the annulus still:

    Tarm=−10×1500300=−50 N mT_{arm} = -\frac{10 \times 1500}{300} = -50\ \text{N m}Tarm​=−30010×1500​=−50 N m
  4. Step 4Find the holding torque

    Torque balance:

    TA=−(TS+Tarm)=−(10−50)=40 N mT_A = -(T_S + T_{arm}) = -(10 - 50) = 40\ \text{N m}TA​=−(TS​+Tarm​)=−(10−50)=40 N m

Answer 96 teeth; arm at 300 rpm in the sun's direction (a 5 to 1 reduction); 50 N m out; the casing holds 40 N m.

Short problems

5.BA pair has a path of contact of 25 mm, module 6 mm and ϕ=20∘\phi = 20^\circϕ=20∘. Find the contact ratio.

    pb=πmcos⁡ϕ=π×6×0.9397=17.71 mmp_b = \pi m\cos\phi = \pi \times 6 \times 0.9397 = 17.71\ \text{mm}pb​=πmcosϕ=π×6×0.9397=17.71 mm

5.CFind the fewest teeth on a 20° full-depth pinion meshing with a rack without undercut.

5.DA sun of 20 teeth and planets of 30 teeth need an annulus of how many teeth?

  1. Step 1Span the gap
    TA=TS+2TP=20+60=80T_A = T_S + 2T_P = 20 + 60 = 80TA​=TS​+2TP​=20+60=80

Answer 80 teeth.

5.EA car takes a bend with its left wheel at 180 rpm and right wheel at 220 rpm. Find the speed of the differential cage (crown wheel).

Term: Differential: lets the two driven wheels turn at different speeds on a bend.

  1. Step 1Average the wheel speeds
    Ncage=180+2202=200 rpmN_{cage} = \frac{180 + 220}{2} = 200\ \text{rpm}Ncage​=2180+220​=200 rpm

Answer 200 rpm.

Problem 7.1 Speed change of an open-arm Watt governor

In an open-arm governor the arms are 400 mm long and hinged 25 mm either side of the axis. Find the percentage change of speed when the arm angle θ\thetaθ to the vertical falls from 35° to 30°.

Rattan (2009), Example 16.1

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Arm lengthlll400 mm
Hinge offseteee25 mm
Arm anglesθ\thetaθ35° and 30°

Find

  • Percentage change of speed

Terms used in this problem

Governor
a device that senses engine speed with spinning balls and moves a sleeve to adjust the fuel supply.
Height hhh
the vertical distance from the ball centres down (or up) to where the arms, produced, meet the spindle axis.
Sleeve
the collar that slides on the spindle as the balls rise and fall.
Open arms
arms hinged off the axis, so the arms produced meet the axis below the hinges.
Watt governor law
for a ball on an arm, h=g/ω2h = g/\omega^2h=g/ω2; with NNN in rpm and hhh in m, h=895/N2h = 895/N^2h=895/N2.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the height at each angle

    The arm gives lcos⁡θl\cos\thetalcosθ, and the offset adds ecot⁡θe\cot\thetaecotθ down to the meeting point.

    h=lcos⁡θ+ecot⁡θh = l\cos\theta + e\cot\thetah=lcosθ+ecotθ
    h35=327.7+35.7=363.4 mm,h30=346.4+43.3=389.7 mmh_{35} = 327.7 + 35.7 = 363.4\ \text{mm},\qquad h_{30} = 346.4 + 43.3 = 389.7\ \text{mm}h35​=327.7+35.7=363.4 mm,h30​=346.4+43.3=389.7 mm
  2. Step 2Find the speeds
    N=895h:N35=49.63 rpm,N30=47.92 rpmN = \sqrt{\frac{895}{h}}:\qquad N_{35} = 49.63\ \text{rpm},\qquad N_{30} = 47.92\ \text{rpm}N=h895​​:N35​=49.63 rpm,N30​=47.92 rpm
  3. Step 3Find the change
    N30N35=363.4389.7=0.966,fall 3.44%\frac{N_{30}}{N_{35}} = \sqrt{\frac{363.4}{389.7}} = 0.966,\qquad \text{fall } 3.44\%N35​N30​​=389.7363.4​​=0.966,fall 3.44%

Answer The speed falls by 3.44%.

Problem 7.2 Speed range of a Porter governor, with and without friction

Each arm of a Porter governor is 200 mm long and pivoted on the axis. The ball radii at the least and greatest speeds are 120 mm and 160 mm. The sleeve has a mass of 24 kg and each ball 4 kg. Find the range of speed, and the range if the sleeve friction is 18 N.

Rattan (2009), Example 16.2

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Arm lengthlll200 mm
Ball radiir1,r2r_1, r_2r1​,r2​120 mm, 160 mm
Ball massmmm4 kg
Sleeve massMMM24 kg
Sleeve frictionfff18 N

Find

  • Speed range without and with friction

Terms used in this problem

Governor
a device that senses engine speed with spinning balls and moves a sleeve to adjust the fuel supply.
Height hhh
the vertical distance from the ball centres down (or up) to where the arms, produced, meet the spindle axis.
Sleeve
the collar that slides on the spindle as the balls rise and fall.
Porter governor
a Watt governor with a heavy central sleeve load MMM, which raises the speed for the same height.
Sleeve friction fff
resists sleeve movement: it lowers the speed at which the sleeve falls and raises the speed at which it rises.

Solution

  1. Step 1Find the heights
    h=l2−r2:h1=160 mm,h2=120 mmh = \sqrt{l^2 - r^2}:\qquad h_1 = 160\ \text{mm},\qquad h_2 = 120\ \text{mm}h=l2−r2​:h1​=160 mm,h2​=120 mm
  2. Step 2Find the speeds without friction

    Equal arms on the axis:

    N2=895h⋅m+MmN^2 = \frac{895}{h}\cdot\frac{m + M}{m}N2=h895​⋅mm+M​
    N1=197.9 rpm,N2=228.5 rpm,range 30.6 rpmN_1 = 197.9\ \text{rpm},\qquad N_2 = 228.5\ \text{rpm},\qquad \text{range } 30.6\ \text{rpm}N1​=197.9 rpm,N2​=228.5 rpm,range 30.6 rpm
  3. Step 3Add friction

    Lowest speed: sleeve falling, load Mg−fMg - fMg−f, at r1r_1r1​. Highest: sleeve rising, load Mg+fMg + fMg+f, at r2r_2r2​.

    N2=895h⋅mg+Mg∓fmgN^2 = \frac{895}{h}\cdot\frac{mg + Mg \mp f}{mg}N2=h895​⋅mgmg+Mg∓f​
    N1=191.3 rpm,N2=235.9 rpm,range 44.6 rpmN_1 = 191.3\ \text{rpm},\qquad N_2 = 235.9\ \text{rpm},\qquad \text{range } 44.6\ \text{rpm}N1​=191.3 rpm,N2​=235.9 rpm,range 44.6 rpm

Answer 197.9 to 228.5 rpm (30.6 rpm) without friction; 191.3 to 235.9 rpm (44.6 rpm) with 18 N of friction.

Problem 7.3 Spring for a Hartnell governor

A Hartnell governor has balls of 2 kg, ball arms of 100 mm and sleeve arms of 60 mm. The ball radius is 100 mm at 300 rpm and 130 mm at 315 rpm. Neglecting the sleeve mass, find the spring stiffness and initial compression, and say whether the governor is stable.

Given

QuantitySymbolValue
Ball massmmm2 kg
Ball armxxx100 mm
Sleeve armyyy60 mm
Lowest position100 mm at 300 rpm
Highest position130 mm at 315 rpm

Find

  • Spring stiffness sss
  • Initial compression
  • Stability

Terms used in this problem

Hartnell governor
a spring-loaded governor: bell-crank levers carry the balls, and a spring on the spindle pushes the sleeve down.
Bell-crank lever
an L-shaped lever with a ball arm xxx and a sleeve arm yyy.
Lift
how far the sleeve rises between the lowest and highest positions.
Controlling force FcF_cFc​
the inward force needed on each ball to keep it on its circle, mω2rm\omega^2 rmω2r.
Stable governor
one where the radius rises as the speed rises; the controlling-force line, extended, cuts the force axis below the origin.

Solution

  1. Step 1Convert the speeds
    ω1=31.42 rad/s,ω2=32.99 rad/s\omega_1 = 31.42\ \text{rad/s},\qquad \omega_2 = 32.99\ \text{rad/s}ω1​=31.42 rad/s,ω2​=32.99 rad/s
  2. Step 2Find the spring force at each position

    Moments about the lever pivot for two balls: S=2mω2r (x/y)S = 2m\omega^2 r\,(x/y)S=2mω2r(x/y).

    S1=2×2×0.10×31.422×10060=658 NS_1 = 2 \times 2 \times 0.10 \times 31.42^2 \times \tfrac{100}{60} = 658\ \text{N}S1​=2×2×0.10×31.422×60100​=658 N
    S2=2×2×0.13×32.992×10060=943 NS_2 = 2 \times 2 \times 0.13 \times 32.99^2 \times \tfrac{100}{60} = 943\ \text{N}S2​=2×2×0.13×32.992×60100​=943 N
  3. Step 3Find the lift and stiffness
    lift=(130−100)×60100=18 mm,s=943−65818=15.8 N/mm\text{lift} = (130 - 100) \times \frac{60}{100} = 18\ \text{mm},\qquad s = \frac{943 - 658}{18} = 15.8\ \text{N/mm}lift=(130−100)×10060​=18 mm,s=18943−658​=15.8 N/mm

Solution, continued

  1. Step 4Find the initial compression
    S1s=65815.8=41.5 mm\frac{S_1}{s} = \frac{658}{15.8} = 41.5\ \text{mm}sS1​​=15.8658​=41.5 mm
  2. Step 5Check stability

    Controlling force per ball at each radius, then extend the line to r=0r = 0r=0.

    F1=2×0.10×31.422=197 N,F2=2×0.13×32.992=283 NF_1 = 2 \times 0.10 \times 31.42^2 = 197\ \text{N},\qquad F_2 = 2 \times 0.13 \times 32.99^2 = 283\ \text{N}F1​=2×0.10×31.422=197 N,F2​=2×0.13×32.992=283 N
    F(0)=197−283−19730×100=−88 N<0F(0) = 197 - \frac{283 - 197}{30} \times 100 = -88\ \text{N} < 0F(0)=197−30283−197​×100=−88 N<0

Answer Spring of 15.8 N/mm with 41.5 mm initial compression. The intercept is negative, so the governor is stable.
